Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Elk Minimum Total Count Survey of WMU 732 (CFB Suffield) and the 
Surrounding Elk Range (2022) 
Background 
Canadian Forces Base Suffield (CFB Suffield), located north of Medicine Hat, covers an area of approximately 2,700 km2. This 
includes a 458 km2 designated National Wildlife Area (NWA), one of the largest spans of ecologically unique and intact native 
prairie in Canada. A herd of less than 300 elk were translocated from Elk Island National Park to CFB Suffield in 1997 and 
1998. This effort aimed to reestablish the once prevalent ungulate to the landscape and improve grassland health using a 
native grazer. With natural predators absent from the landscape, the herd increased to over 7000 head. The effect of 
uncontrolled herd expansion caused conflict with farmers and livestock producers regarding damage to annual crops and 
property adjacent to the military base. In 2012, the first elk hunt in Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 732 (CFB Suffield) 
commenced. A hunting season for elk has continued yearly as part of AEP and CFB Suffield’s elk herd management program 
to reduce and maintain the elk population at a manageable level (ECCC 2021). 
WMU 732 is a federally owned military base that is closed off to access by the general public. The WMU and adjacent lands 
are within Alberta’s dry mixedgrass natural subregion. Land within the base is used for military operations, training, and 
material testing. Some portions of Suffield also allow seasonal grazing by a local grazing co-op. A large amount of oil and gas 
development is also present. Surrounding land use is agricultural, including annual crop production and cattle grazing (the 
majority of which is community pastures or grazing leases on Crown land). 
An aerial survey to determine the status of the Suffield elk population is conducted periodically within WMU 732 and adjacent 
lands known to be used by the elk herd. This is the third elk survey conducted in the WMU since the elk hunt started. The most 
recent survey occurred in 2019 (Table 1). 
The objective of the February 2022 survey was to assess the status of the elk population in WMU 732 and surrounding area 
by determining population size and age-sex composition. Additionally updated population numbers will be used to confirm the 
progress of elk hunting in controlling population growth. 
Survey method 
A transect based rotary wing aerial survey was conducted from February 16 to 18, 2022, using a minimum total count design 
to survey elk within their known range. Survey area included full coverage of WMU 732, with a significant buffer of adjacent 
provincial lands, including portions of WMU’s 150, 144, 148, 124, and 128. Sixty-one east-west transects were flown on each 
minute of latitude (1.85 km spaced). Altitude was generally in the range of 400–600 feet above ground level, in order to 
optimize sightability of elk. Due to the high visibility of elk in a mainly treeless landscape, even without ideal snow cover, 
survey coverage was assumed to be 100%. Thus is assumed all elk were detected during the WMU 732 survey. Elk are 
generally found in herds during the winter months, also increasing their visibility. Observers routinely detected elk well beyond 
the 1.85 km survey buffer. While it is possible a small number of elk were missed by surveyors while flying, the impact of a 
few potentially overlooked individuals on the total number of elk is negligible. Elk abundance was reported as a minimum total 
count. 
 
At each observation point, elk were confirmed and, and when possible, sex and age was recorded. Antler size for bulls was 
classified as “small” (spike or two points on one or both antlers), “medium” (antlers with 3 or more points), or “large” (antlers 
with ≥ 5 points). Digital single-lens reflex (DSLR) cameras were used to photograph large herds to analyze after the survey, in 
order to increase classification accuracy while maintaining survey efficiency. In the instances where a herd could not be 
accurately classified due to poor image quality and large herd size, sex and age composition was estimated by deriving a ratio 
from mixed composition herd photos that could be classified with confidence by surveyors. Thus the resulting bull:cow:calf 
ratios are estimates. However, the minimum total count of elk observed during the survey is accurate, as individual elk were

Appendix A: Survey Flight Plan for WMU 732 (CFB Suffield) and the Surrounding Elk Range. 
 
Due to restricted airspace for military operations, surveying was only permitted within CFB Suffield airspace during specified 
time windows. This access was facilitated by staff submitting a prior permission request for approval to Suffield range control 
to enter the airspace for the purposes of the survey. For this reason, optimal snow cover was not possible for the entire area 
when planning survey dates, and additional ungulate species were also not surveyed in the surrounding WMU’s. 
Results 
A total of 2,472 elk were observed during the survey among 26 groups (range 2 to 1,073), representing a 9% reduction from 
results in 2019 (Table 1). The bull:cow:calf ratio was 19:100:37. Of the 301 antlered bulls observed during the survey, 173 
(58%) were classified as small, 88 (29%) were classified as medium, and 40 (13%) were classified as large. 
The largest herd observed during the survey totalled 1073 elk, and was located northwest of Dishpan Lake in the northwest of 
WMU 732. Due to poor image quality, the herd could not be confidently and accurately classified from photographs, thus herd 
classification was estimated to be 730 cows, 268 calves, and 75 bulls. The second largest herd count was also located in 
WMU 732 near the coulees northwest of Whitehorse Lake, and totalled 540 elk. Likewise, the herd classification estimate was 
derived from ratios of other herds due to poor image quality, with an estimate of 367 cows, 135 calves, and 38 bulls. Besides 
these very large herds, other groups ranged from two to 390 individuals. For all observation results and herd composition, 
refer to Appendix B: Minimum Total Count and Herd Composition of Elk Observed from WMU 732 (CFB Suffield) and the 
Surrounding Elk Range. 
Ninety percent (90%) of the elk observed were recorded within WMU 732 (20 of the 26 observations), and the majority of 
these observations occurred in the northeast quadrant of the WMU, including the three largest herds. The remaining 10% of 
observations were recorded in WMUs 150, 148, and 144. For a map of all elk observations and their locations, refer to 
Appendix C: Observation Locations of Elk in WMU 732 (CFB Suffield) and the Surrounding Elk Range. 
The results of the February 2022 survey show the elk herd at its lowest level since hunting inside CFB Suffield began in 2012. 
This suggests hunting is having the desired effect to reduce elk populations in order to produce lower levels of wildlife conflict 
and sustainability of the range resources on CFB Suffield.
